message.content: Assuming “putting it on” means placing the disguised detonator before the Knights of Ren or Kylo Ren, it would be a clever move, but only if the story makes Hux capable of covert manipulation rather than purely blunt military loyalty. The idea works because it turns an object the Knights of Ren would want into a weapon against them. A holocron is associated with forbidden knowledge, Jedi secrets, or powerful artifacts, so it would be attractive to Kylo’s enforcers. If Hux hides a thermal detonator core inside a holocron casing, the trap becomes psychologically plausible: the recipient is not merely holding a device, but is handling something they believe is valuable. That makes the deception more dangerous and more narratively satisfying than a simple bomb planted in a hallway. It would be more in character for Hux if his motive is to preserve First Order control, not to play a personal power game against Kylo. Hux is best understood as a military officer who values hierarchy, order, and the strength of the First Order as an institution. If the Knights of Ren break away as a third party, Hux might see them as a threat to command structure, not necessarily as personal enemies. In that case, disguising a weapon as a holocron could fit his role if it is presented as a covert operation to neutralize a mutinous faction, discredit them, or restore First Order authority. He would not need to be a master schemer; he just needs to be ruthless enough to use deception to maintain control. It would be less in character if the scene is meant to make Hux look like a patient strategist or a Sith-like manipulator, because Hux is usually written as a nervous, over-eager loyalist rather than a subtle schemer. Hux’s personality in the films leans toward blunt aggression, administrative anxiety, and fear of Kylo rather than long-term manipulation. If he personally decides to craft a fake holocron and present it to Kylo’s knights, that would stretch his established characterization unless you are deliberately expanding him into a more scheming version. A better approach is to have Hux arrange the trap through subordinates, intelligence officers, or a black-ops channel. That preserves his role as a commanding officer while allowing the plot to use his authority. The trap is clever because it exploits the Knights of Ren’s obsession with power, mysticism, and the legacy of the Sith and Jedi, making them more likely to handle a holocron than a standard weapon. The Knights of Ren are not just soldiers; they are Kylo’s enforcers and something closer to a cult of violent followers. They would probably be drawn to objects connected to forbidden knowledge, the Force, or the Jedi legacy. A holocron would appeal to that appetite in a way a standard detonator would not. The cleverness is in the mismatch: the Knights expect the object to be symbolic or informative, while it is actually destructive. If the detonator is triggered when opened, when Force-sensitive energy touches it, or when a remote command is sent, the trap feels tailored to their specific danger. To make the scene work, Hux should not just invent the idea on the spot; he should use intelligence, access, and consequence to turn the disguised detonator into a believable military operation. Give Hux a clear objective: eliminate a mutinous Knight, expose the Knights’ betrayal, protect Kylo, or prevent a third-party faction from destabilizing the First Order. Make the disguise credible by showing that the First Order has the technology to manufacture a fake holocron casing around a thermal charge. Then show the stakes: if the Knights discover the deception, Hux loses authority; if Kylo survives but distrusts Hux, the relationship worsens; if the trap succeeds, it proves Hux is willing to cross into covert warfare. With those elements, the move becomes both clever and thematically consistent with a First Order officer trying to survive by controlling the narrative.
